steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper GC-SNTK, a fast graph condensation method that replaces bi-level GNN training with kernel ridge regression using a structure-based neural tangent kernel. Motivate graph condensation, explain the problems with existing bi-level methods and the challenges of a KRR formulation, introduce the framework, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Graph data, GNNs and the cost of training on large graphs
2. Dataset condensation and bi-level graph condensation
3. Limitations of bi-level methods
4. Reformulating as KRR and its two challenges
5. GC-SNTK and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- internet technology -> lots of graph-structured data, used in Web applications
- e.g. social networks (cite), semantic networks (cite) -> nodes and edges
- GNNs (cite), advanced DNNs, attention for graph mining tasks in past few years
- success relies on large-scale datasets (cite)
- training on them needs enormous resources (power, memory storage, GPU runtime) due to thousands of training iterations, hyper-parameter optimization, neural architecture search (cite)

2. Dataset condensation
- data-centric approach: condense large graph datasets into smaller, information-rich synthetic versions (cite)
- Dataset Condensation (DC) a.k.a. dataset distillation (cite): small synthetic version, keeps prediction performance, image domain
- example: 10 images distilled from MNIST (cite) with 60,000 images -> 94% accuracy, 95% of full dataset performance (cite)
- early efforts on graphs (cite)
- vanilla graph condensation (cite) = bi-level optimization (Figure 1): condense whole graph into small graph of few nodes + features via matching objectives between two GNNs
- Figure 2(a): outer synthetic graph optimization (outer loop) relies on inner GNN trained on synthetic graph (inner loop) (cite)

3. Limitations
- intrinsic limitations: unstable training (cite), massive computation costs (cite) -> inferior synthesized data
- generalization across GNN architectures needs multiple parameter initialization (cite) -> three nested loops, substantial time

4. KRR reformulation
- reformulate graph condensation as Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR), closed-form solution (cite), instead of multi-iteration inner GNN training in bi-level optimization
- KRR ~ classification task, depends on kernel function for similarity matrix among instances
- vanilla kernels (dot product, polynomial) may hinder expressiveness for complex node relationships
- challenge 1: design appropriate kernel for graph condensation in KRR
- graph data non-Euclidean, complex dependencies among nodes; need topological signals in non-linear kernel space
- challenge 2: use topological structure to improve kernel design in KRR

5. GC-SNTK
- Graph Condensation with Structure-Based Neural Tangent Kernel (GC-SNTK), node classification
- estimated neural kernel in KRR = training infinite-width neural networks through infinite steps of SGD
- Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel (SNTK): neighborhood aggregation -> high-quality condensed graph
- contributions:
  - principled KRR-based way to improve condensation efficiency, replacing inner GNN training (inner loop) by SNTK
  - GC-SNTK synthesizes smaller graph efficiently; various GNN architectures trained on it keep comparable generalization
  - extensive experiments on various datasets: effectiveness, efficiency, generalization across GNN architectures

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Because internet technology is so widespread, a large amount of graph-structured data has been accumulated, and this data is widely used in Web applications. For example, social networks and semantic networks can naturally be represented as graphs made of nodes and edges. Since graph-structured data is used so extensively, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which are one of the advanced Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), have got a lot of attention in the past few years for their performance on various graph mining tasks. The remarkable success of most existing GNNs relies largely on large-scale datasets. Training GNNs on these large-scale datasets is effective but still difficult, because it usually needs enormous computational resources (e.g., power, memory storage, GPU runtime, etc.) because of thousands of training iterations, hyper-parameters optimization, and neural architecture search.

One data-centric approach to these challenges is to condense the original large-scale graph datasets into synthesized versions that are smaller but still information-rich. Dataset Condensation (DC), also called dataset distillation, is one of the most advanced paradigms, and it has achieved remarkable performance in getting a small-scale synthetic version of the full dataset while keeping models’ prediction performance in the image domain. For instance, 10 images distilled from the whole MNIST dataset, which has 60,000 images, are enough to achieve a 94% accuracy, which is 95% of the performance of the full dataset. Recently, early efforts have explored dataset condensation on graph-structured data. As shown in Figure 1, the vanilla graph condensation methods can be formulated as a bi-level optimization problem, which condenses the entire graph into a small graph of a few nodes with their features using various matching objectives between two GNNs models. As illustrated in Figure 2(a), the outer synthetic graph optimization (i.e., outer loop) relies heavily on the inner GNN model that is trained on the synthetic graph (i.e., inner loop).

3. Limitations
- intrinsic limitations: unstable training (cite), massive computation costs (cite) -> inferior synthesized data
- generalization across GNN architectures needs multiple parameter initialization (cite) -> three nested loops, substantial time

4. KRR reformulation
- reformulate graph condensation as Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR), closed-form solution (cite), instead of multi-iteration inner GNN training in bi-level optimization
- KRR ~ classification task, depends on kernel function for similarity matrix among instances
- vanilla kernels (dot product, polynomial) may hinder expressiveness for complex node relationships
- challenge 1: design appropriate kernel for graph condensation in KRR
- graph data non-Euclidean, complex dependencies among nodes; need topological signals in non-linear kernel space
- challenge 2: use topological structure to improve kernel design in KRR

5. GC-SNTK
- Graph Condensation with Structure-Based Neural Tangent Kernel (GC-SNTK), node classification
- estimated neural kernel in KRR = training infinite-width neural networks through infinite steps of SGD
- Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel (SNTK): neighborhood aggregation -> high-quality condensed graph
- contributions:
  - principled KRR-based way to improve condensation efficiency, replacing inner GNN training (inner loop) by SNTK
  - GC-SNTK synthesizes smaller graph efficiently; various GNN architectures trained on it keep comparable generalization
  - extensive experiments on various datasets: effectiveness, efficiency, generalization across GNN architectures

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Because internet technology is so widespread, a large amount of graph-structured data has been accumulated, and this data is widely used in Web applications. For example, social networks and semantic networks can naturally be represented as graphs made of nodes and edges. Since graph-structured data is used so extensively, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which are one of the advanced Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), have got a lot of attention in the past few years for their performance on various graph mining tasks. The remarkable success of most existing GNNs relies largely on large-scale datasets. Training GNNs on these large-scale datasets is effective but still difficult, because it usually needs enormous computational resources (e.g., power, memory storage, GPU runtime, etc.) because of thousands of training iterations, hyper-parameters optimization, and neural architecture search.

One data-centric approach to these challenges is to condense the original large-scale graph datasets into synthesized versions that are smaller but still information-rich. Dataset Condensation (DC), also called dataset distillation, is one of the most advanced paradigms, and it has achieved remarkable performance in getting a small-scale synthetic version of the full dataset while keeping models’ prediction performance in the image domain. For instance, 10 images distilled from the whole MNIST dataset, which has 60,000 images, are enough to achieve a 94% accuracy, which is 95% of the performance of the full dataset. Recently, early efforts have explored dataset condensation on graph-structured data. As shown in Figure 1, the vanilla graph condensation methods can be formulated as a bi-level optimization problem, which condenses the entire graph into a small graph of a few nodes with their features using various matching objectives between two GNNs models. As illustrated in Figure 2(a), the outer synthetic graph optimization (i.e., outer loop) relies heavily on the inner GNN model that is trained on the synthetic graph (i.e., inner loop).

Even with this success, most existing bi-level graph condensation methods have intrinsic limitations such as unstable training and massive computation costs, and this leads to inferior performance in generating synthesized data. Even worse, making sure the condensed data generalizes to various GNN architectures needs multiple parameter initialization, which leads to three complex nested loops in the optimization and takes substantial time.

To tackle these problems, in this paper we propose to reformulate graph condensation as a Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) task with a closed-form solution, instead of training GNNs in the inner loop with multiple iterations to learn synthetic graph data via bi-level optimization. But using KRR for graph condensation has big challenges. The KRR paradigm can be treated as a classification task and it relies heavily on the design of the kernel function that calculates the similarity matrix among instances. The vanilla kernel functions, like dot product and polynomial kernel, might hinder the expressiveness when modeling complex relationships among nodes. So the first challenge is how to design an appropriate kernel function to optimize graph condensation in the KRR paradigm. Also, unlike images or text data, graph-structured data lies in non-Euclidean space and has complex intrinsic dependencies among nodes. This means we need to capture graph topological signals in non-linear kernel space. So the second challenge is how to make effective use of the topological structure in graphs to improve the design of the kernel function in KRR for graph condensation.

In this paper, we introduce a novel dataset condensation framework for graph-structured data in the node classification task, called Graph Condensation with Structure-Based Neural Tangent Kernel (GC-SNTK). The framework uses the power of the estimated neural kernel in the KRR paradigm, which can be seen as training infinite-width neural networks through infinite steps of SGD. Also, to capture the topological structure of graphs, we introduce a Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel (SNTK) that does neighborhood aggregation of nodes to generate a high-quality condensed graph. Our contributions are as follows:

- We propose a principled way based on kernel ridge regression to significantly improve graph condensation efficiency, by replacing the inner GNNs training (i.e., inner loop) with the Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel in the KRR paradigm.

- We propose a novel graph condensation framework GC-SNTK, which can effectively and efficiently synthesize a smaller graph so that various GNN architectures trained on it keep comparable generalization performance while being significantly efficient.

- We conduct extensive experiments on various datasets to show that the proposed framework is effective and efficient for graph condensation. Our method also has powerful generalization capability across various GNN architectures.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The prevalence of internet technology has accumulated a large amount of graph-structured data, which is widely used in Web applications. For example, social networks [1,2,3,4,5] and semantic networks [6,7] can be naturally represented as graphs consisting of nodes and edges. Due to the extensive application of graph-structured data, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [8,9,10], one of the advanced Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), have gained significant attention for their performance on various graph mining tasks during the past few years. Notably, the remarkable achievement of most existing GNNs largely relies on large-scale datasets [11,12]. Despite being effective, training GNNs on such large-scale datasets still presents difficulties, as it usually requires enormous computational resources (e.g., power, memory storage, GPU runtime, etc.) caused by thousands of training iterations, hyper-parameters optimization, and neural architecture search [13,14].

A data-centric approach to these challenges is to condense the original large-scale graph datasets into synthesized, smaller yet information-rich versions [15]. As one of the most advanced paradigms, Dataset Condensation (DC), also known as dataset distillation [16], has achieved remarkable performance in obtaining a small-scale synthetic version of the full dataset while preserving models’ prediction performance in the image domain. For instance, 10 images distilled from the whole MNIST dataset [17] with 60,000 images are sufficient to achieve a 94% accuracy, reaching 95% of the performance of the full dataset [15]. Recently, early efforts have explored the potential of dataset condensation on graph-structured data [14,18]. As shown in Figure 1, the vanilla graph condensation methods [14,18] can be formulated as a bi-level optimization problem that condenses the entire graph into a small graph of a few nodes with corresponding features via various matching objectives between two GNN models. More specifically, as illustrated in Figure 2(a), the outer synthetic graph optimization (i.e., outer loop) heavily relies on the inner GNN model trained on the synthetic graph (i.e., inner loop) [14,18].

Despite this success, most existing bi-level graph condensation methods suffer from intrinsic limitations such as unstable training [19,20] and massive computation costs [21], leading to inferior performance in synthesized data generation. Worse still, ensuring the condensed data’s generalization on various GNN architectures requires multiple parameter initialization [18,14], leading to complex three nested loops in the algorithmic optimization and substantial time consumption.

To tackle these problems, in this paper we propose to reformulate graph condensation as a Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) task with a closed-form solution [22,23], instead of training GNNs (in the inner loop) with multiple iterations to learn synthetic graph data via bi-level optimization. However, leveraging KRR for graph condensation faces tremendous challenges. The KRR paradigm, which can be treated as a classification task, largely relies on the design of kernel functions to calculate the similarity matrix among instances. Vanilla kernel functions, such as the dot product and polynomial kernel, might hinder the expressiveness of modeling complex relationships among nodes. Therefore, the first challenge is how to design an appropriate kernel function for optimizing graph condensation in the KRR paradigm. Moreover, unlike images or text data, graph-structured data lies in non-Euclidean space with complex intrinsic dependencies among nodes; it is therefore imperative to capture graph topological signals in non-linear kernel space. Thus, the second challenge is how to effectively take advantage of the topological structure of graphs to enhance the design of the kernel function in KRR for graph condensation.

In this paper, we introduce a novel dataset condensation framework for graph-structured data in the node classification task, named Graph Condensation with Structure-Based Neural Tangent Kernel (GC-SNTK). More specifically, the framework harnesses the power of the estimated neural kernel in the KRR paradigm, which can be considered as training infinite-width neural networks through infinite steps of SGD. Furthermore, to capture the topological structure of graphs, a Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel (SNTK) is introduced to execute neighborhood aggregation of nodes for generating a high-quality condensed graph. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- We propose a principled way based on kernel ridge regression to significantly improve graph condensation efficiency, achieved by replacing the inner GNN training (i.e., inner loop) with the Structure-based Neural Tangent Kernel in the KRR paradigm.

- We propose a novel graph condensation framework, GC-SNTK, which can effectively and efficiently synthesize a smaller graph so that various GNN architectures trained on top of it maintain comparable generalization performance while being significantly efficient.

- We conduct extensive experiments on various datasets to show the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework for graph condensation. Moreover, our method offers powerful generalization capability across various GNN architectures.
